news_drafts.headline: Liverpool Cabinet papers show £12.217m schools high-needs deficit brought forward from 2025/26
news_drafts.lead:
Liverpool City Council carries a cumulative deficit of £12.217m on the high needs part of its dedicated schools grant, brought forward from 2025/26, according to the medium term financial strategy refresh put to Cabinet on 17 November 2026. The high needs block is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

The dedicated schools grant is the government grant that funds schools, and a deficit on it is an overspend, usually on support for children with special needs. The paper describes the sum as "a cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) high needs deficit of £12.217m brought forward from 2025/26".

The paper says the statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps schools-funding deficits off councils' main revenue budgets, is in place to March 2028. It also says the government has set out an intention to support councils with deficits on the dedicated schools grant through a High Needs Stability Grant. The paper does not give a figure for that grant in the material reviewed.

news_drafts.headline: Liverpool forecasts £26.4m overspend on special needs funding, taking schools deficit to £38.6m
news_drafts.lead:
Liverpool City Council expects to overspend by £26.417m this year on high needs, the part of schools funding that pays for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The forecast, in the second-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) to Cabinet on 13 October, takes the total deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to £38.634m once £12.217m carried forward from 2025/26 is added.

The report says government has signalled a possible High Needs Stability Grant of about £6.917m, equal to 90% of the cumulative deficit to March 2026. Even with that grant, the paper says at least £5.300m would still have to be recovered from the council's General Fund, its main day-to-day budget, with the pressure extending into future years.

The report links the deficit to continuing rises in Education, Health and Care Plans, the legal documents that set out a child's support, and to more demand for places in non-maintained and independent special schools. Specialist provision is also still expanding, which affects capital spending (money spent on things that last) as well as day-to-day costs. SEN transport, which received £13.596m of budget growth, is currently forecast to come in on budget. The paper nonetheless calls it "a key financial risk for the council" and says performance will be monitored closely through the year.

news_drafts.headline: Liverpool council's reserves hit 'very low level' as financial pressures mount
news_drafts.lead:
Liverpool's reserves — money a council sets aside as a financial cushion — have fallen to £25.4m after overspends of £23.8m in 2024/25 and £11.7m in 2025/26. The council's chief finance officer said the council is now holding "a very low level of usable reserves which will reduce the ability of the council to manage its continuing financial challenges going forward."

The overspends were driven by demand-led service pressures: adult social care (£15.3m), children's services (£17.5m), and homelessness and transport (£21.2m). The council forecasts a cumulative budget gap—the difference between expected spending and available funding—of £63.9m by 2028/29. The council has raised council tax by the maximum allowed 4.99% for 2026/27, despite a 5.8% increase in government grant, signalling limited room for further local revenue-raising.

findings.headline: Government plans to share 20% of locally retained Business Rates with Mayoral Strategic Authorities from 2027/28
findings.detail: The paper says councils will see no detriment at the point the system changes, with lost rates returned through central government grant. Future growth will be tapered to 80% to the council to fund the Mayoral Strategic Authority's share.
findings.matters: A change in how business rates growth is shared alters the return on growth for every council in a combined authority area.
findings.figures: 20% of locally retained Business Rates to Mayoral Strategic Authorities from 2027/28; growth tapered to 80%
findings.quote: plans to share 20% of locally retained Business Rates with Mayoral Strategic Authorities (MSAs) from 2027/28

findings.headline: Fees and charges income of £35.47m was achieved year to date to October 2026, 6% above the same point in 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper says the programme now tracks fees and charges income monthly against profiled budget and previous-year income. Against 2024/25, the year-to-date figure is 18% higher.
findings.matters: Income running ahead of the prior year is evidence that fees and charges measures are landing, which bears on the income assumptions in other councils' budgets.
findings.figures: £35.47m fees and charges income year to date to October 2026; 6% above 2025/26 at the same point; 18% above 2024/25; 3.1% CPI uplift; £1.563m full-year effect
findings.quote: As at October 2026, £35.47m of fees and charges income has been achieved financial year to date, which is 6% higher than achieved at the same point in 2025/26

findings.headline: Over 550 of up to 1,500 contracted temporary housing units were supplied by end September 2026, after the contract start was brought forward from October to end July 2026
findings.detail: The four housing providers are required to transition 50% of the properties secured to permanent accommodation within 12 months. The paper says the council is negotiating earlier transition dates, and the contracted rates are discounted against previous rates for identical properties.
findings.matters: A contract capacity figure and a bring-forward start date show how a council is reducing reliance on nightly-paid accommodation, which a finance director at another council facing the same costs would compare.
findings.figures: up to 1,500 self-contained units contracted; over 550 units supplied to end September 2026
findings.quote: This new arrangement was set to run from October 2026, but HSS managed to successfully negotiate an earlier start date allowing the council to begin accessing these properties from the end of July 2026.

findings.headline: Families in temporary accommodation are close to 2,300 per night, against an MTFS assumption of approximately 1,600 per night to the end of September 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the interventions have constrained the increase in homelessness costs but have been offset by a rise in families presenting as homeless. It says homelessness remains a significant financial risk because demand drives cost.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are demand-led, so a figure running well above the modelled level shows where a finance director's assumptions are being tested.
findings.figures: approximately 1,600 families per night (MTFS assumption); close to 2,300 families per night (actual)
findings.quote: A key MTFS assumption was that the number of families requiring TA would be approximately 1,600 per night to the end of September.

findings.headline: Children in care stood at 1,258 children in October 2026, down 37 children since March 2026
findings.detail: The paper says numbers have plateaued during 2026/27 to date. Liverpool's rate of 145 per 10,000 children compares with a Core Cities average of 85 and a statistical neighbour average of 120.
findings.matters: Children looked after numbers drive the cost of high-cost external placements, so a reduction is a direct test of the savings built into the MTFS.
findings.figures: 1,258 children in care in October 2026; 75 unaccompanied asylum-seeking children; reduction of 37 children since March 2026; 145 per 10,000 children
findings.quote: The number of children in care in October 2026 was 1,258, including 75 Unaccompanied Asylum-Seeking Children (UASC). This is a reduction of 37 since March 2026

daily_post.headline: Cunard Building heat network connection has October 2026 deadline with council describing timescales as challenging and flagging significant financial risk if deadline is missed
daily_post.lead: Infrastructure schemes with fixed external deadlines carry binary delivery risk. A missed deadline creates unfunded capital or revenue costs, and lenders track such schemes as specific execution risks within the capital programme.
